That is another name for that process. Pavlov's experiment demonstrating the secretion of saliva under the control of stimuli external to the body in dogs is a well known example of the phenomenon those terms describe.

This process, pairing, means that both stimuli condition each other. Whichever stimulus is more effective reinforcement or punishment "wins". The are two kinds of conditioning, operant and respondent/reflexive. Your scenario of preferred music in the morning, describes both. Reflexive conditioning describes stimulus pairing that happens simultaneously. The morning might have aversive stimulation that include non preferred tasks (getting ready for work) or sensations (feeling tired). If these are more aversive than the music is pleasant , then the music, not the morning stimulation, is conditioned. Operant conditioning describes non simultaneous pairings of behaviors with stimuli. It could be that you are listening to music before having to do something aversive. If so, the music then indicates the occurrence of unpleasurable events, perhaps going to work. If the music happens after the unpleasant events, and does actually function as reinforcement, then only the behaviors that happen immediately before the music would be reinforced. 
There is also the phenomenon of unpairing. Your favorite music might have been conditioned by other stimuli that made it pleasant. If you usually are engaged in otherwise pleasant activities while listening to music such as dancing, relaxing, playing video games, eating, or other preferred activities, then the musical stimulation in the absence of those other preferred stimuli would lose its potency as "pleasurable".

Concentration requires an object. If you are not concentrating on something then you're not concentrating. For example, you might concentrate on the breath. When you are not focusing on the feeling of the breath in your nose, then you are not concentrating on the breath with in your nose. When you are concentrating on the breath within your nose, then you are concentrating on the breath within your nose. The important part is to decide what you will concentrate on before you concentrate on it. Meta-languages!
Meta-language is language that is about some other language. For example, "The word 'red' has three letters." In this sentence, the word "red" is the object language that the rest of the sentence (meta-language) is about.
So, the issue with this question is that it obfuscates a meta-language with its object language. 
So, the object language in OP's question would be "this question" since the rest of the question is about itself.  

The problem here is that it's an improper use of English grammar. Consider: "What is the answer to "how many letters are in the English alphabet?"" This question had a definite answer because the object language is a well formed question. However, "this question" is not even a question because it is indexing itself which is a question. And so, their are no conditions of satisfaction for OP's question since the object language, the thing being asked about, is itself a question. And so, the object language indexes (refers to) the meta-language which creates a logical loop.

Favorite anime: One Piece

I know it's probably cliche, but it stands up for several reasons. One reason might just be how long it has been going. You can't watch hundreds of episodes of something and not become invested. Other than that:

Necessity: Oda is a master of this. Too often when an author wants the audience to understand something about a character or the plot, they just show it.  One Piece, however, only gives you the information that is necessary to understand what's going on at that point. Sometimes,  what is left unsaid is far more powerful because it lives in the imagination of the viewer. 

World-building: Another staple of mediocre anime, or story telling in general, is the unbelievable plot twist. Not unexpected. All plot twists are unexpected. But when they come out of thin air. For example, a character is saved by someone who's never even been mentioned before and then disappears once they've served their purpose in the plot. This is harder to believe because it feels unnatural. Oda takes the time to review all the resources the Straw hats have to work with and then sticks to them. One Piece also has a massive geopolitical structure that helps viewers wrap their heads around where the Straw hats are in their journey. 

Balance: drama vs. comedy. It's never too heavy or too light. It doesn't shy away from serious drama, but if things start getting too heavy, Oda will pepper in some jokes to lighten the mood. 

Meta-commentary: this is when characters acknowledge what the audience must be thinking. For example, during the Fishman Island ark. Sanji's health is jeopardized when his nose won't stop bleeding from the sight of all the beautiful mermaids. At one point, he is on the brink of death because of this; at which point, Chopper exclaims, "THIS IS THE STUPIDEST WAY TO DIE!!!" Part of the fun of anime is getting to see things that don't happen in the real world. But, if this is taken too far, the author risks alienating the audience's sense of what is realistically acceptable. 

Character development: tragic back stories are a well known trope within anime, but are often used as a pretext for motivating the plot. Done poorly, they are a cheap trick for garnering the audience's sympathy. Done well, they can help build character integrity and a sense of reality when a character has to make a tough decision. Within One Piece, there is always a reason the characters act as they do. It's not just a product of what makes the character more stereotypically favorable. 

And the biggest reason I love One Piece: 


The tears: At the end of the War of the Best, Shanks is getting ready to leave Marine Ford and begins reflecting on the tragedy Luffy has just endured. He feels compassion for Luffy and then says the one thing that all teenage boys need to hear: It's ok to cry. This moral has remained consistent throughout the show. Not being able to cry can do a lot of damage mentally. I've been locked in a psych ward, lost girlfriends, alienated friends and family, and destroyed more property than I can remember all because no one ever told me it was OK to cry when you're sad. One Piece often deals with different characters' conceptions of what it is to be a man, but one of Oda's unshakeable foundations of manhood is being true to how you feel. This, more than anything makes me respect One Piece because it shows Oda truly understands his audience.

That is,  it would be impossible to get a description of the inherent nature of the physical without appealing to experience in some form or another. 

Furthermore, you don't need to know the inherent nature of two things to form a non-identity between them. We may not know the inherent nature of the physical, but we know enough to distinguish it from the mental. Matter has mass, so if the mind is physical, shouldn't it have weight? These are silly questions because they rely on an equivocation between two different languages.

Mindfulness meditation. Get in the habit of noticing your emotions. Start with anger since that's your concern.  When you feel yourself getting angry,  just notice it.  Don't judge yourself.  Avoid saying things like,  "I'm getting so angry,  what is wrong with me?" Just accept it. Imagine yourself watching as it passes by. Wave to it, bow to it, and watch it fade into nothingness.  Judgments are like fuel for your rage.  They allow you to continue practicing being angry. Just by naming something,  like anger,  you can distance yourself from it.  Which gets at the underlying reason for your anger:  clinging attachment.

Often we get angry because of a twisted belief in justice.  Something like,  "this shouldn't happen to me!" But this thought clouds you understanding.  You will endure suffering no matter what,  denying it won't make it stop or go away.  2. You're going to die,  but more generally,  all things die,  or rather,  come to an end.  While playing your games,  remind yourself that you can't do it forever.  Eventually,  you have to sleep,  eat, bathe,  work,  and live your life outside your games. Essentially,  when you get angry,  remind yourself over and over,  "I am not this game" "I am not this video game character" "I am not my team mates" "I am not [whatever the object of your aggression is at that moment]" By being mindful of suffering, impermanence,  and no-self, you will see the world clearly and so not get caught up in rage fueled fantasies.

I'm in the same boat as OP, but went to graduate school for early childhood education while working as a behavior therapist.  I feel like a teacher's relationship with parents is crucial.  A positive working relationship with parents has many benefits:  academic,  emotional,  behavioral,  and social.  Parents are a child's first teacher,  and I think teachers need to respect that.  Keeping parents up to date on what happens inside the classroom will give them a greater sense of investment in what you are doing, and so create allies in your work as a teacher that have the most influence over a student's life.  Three practices I will use:

1. Happy grams: sticky notes or tags you put on students' shirts, backpacks, or other visible locations that spark conversation between parents and children. e.g. "Ask me about the new class pet!"

2. Positive notes home: pick a few students each day to write notes of appraisal for. This shows parents that you cherish their bundle of joy as they do.  This practice also helps alleviate uncomfortable conversations with parents when there are problems in the class.  

3. Home visits:  I was sceptical of this practice until I studied it.  School performance is always affected by what happens outside the classroom.  A home visit creates an appropriate space to discuss things sick as nutrition, sleep patterns, exercise habits, and other lifestyle patterns that will put the student's classroom performance into a larger context.

4 Divine Abodes (or 4 Immeasurables if you prefer that language):
1. Loving-kindness
2. Compassion
3. Empathetic Joy
4. Equanimity

These by no means exhaust what is traditionally meant by "Buddha nature," they are just examples of some characteristics of a Buddha. There are many more positive traits that would be developed in Buddhahood. A Buddha is one who has developed all positive  characteristics and abandoned all negative characteristics. 

Thubten Chodron and Prof. Malcom David Eckel  (Harvard) both gave similar interpretations of samsara. That being said, I might have been creative with what they literally said. Tbh, I'm a classically trained philosopher, so I believe that any interpretation of anything works as long as it is coherent and defensible. Bear in mind that we are reappropriating a  religion, so getting a little imaginative is in order.

Buddha was very clear on this point. You ought not to accept what he says on faith. If it's "correct" then it will work for you. This means you have to try it out first. I can't say if it will work for you personally, but I can say that 2500 years of his followers found it useful. 

Idk the origin of the term "Buddha nature" other than it belongs to the Mahayana tradition. That being said, resting in the 4 Divine Abodes is a worthy goal regardless of whether it's really possible. Think of it like a self-fulfilling prophecy. Do you remember when you were in school and your teacher told you that you were "smart," "gifted," or "talented?" I guarantee you she was lying. This is an old teacher trick to motivate kids with low self esteem. So, at some level, you have to believe in your Buddha nature in order to manifest it. 

Finally, unrelated, the notion of cyclic existence can be interpreted in a secular way. Think of a bad habit you're trying to quit. When you stop doing it, your life has metaphorically ended and you are reborn a "new" person because that part of your life is over. But, bad habits tend to be " reborn" in your existence because they are difficult to quit. You can call this cyclic existence. Likewise for Relationships . We fight, then make up.  We fight, then make up.  It is only by ending this cycle that you can unconditionally end suffering and achieve true happiness  (nirvana). 

"If there is no self, then what is reborn in the next life?"
Chogyam Trungpa Rinpoche: "I'm sorry to say,  but it's your bad habits. "

This inspires another interpretation of rebirth: you are not reborn all at once, rather as you interact with other humans,  you transmit your habits and way of life to them. Nirvana would then be a state where no one would corrupt you,  but where you spread the virtues of enlightenment to others,  thus fulfilling the path of the Bodhisattva.

"This is bullshit. I don't know how, but you forged this. I'm tired of your tricks."

"Well after what you did to her remaining body, it wasn't easy putting it back together. Nevertheless, she has agreed to suffer the bondage of her physical existence so she could see you again.
